A quick post about a phrase that has proven useful in teaching statistics.


::: {.cell}

:::



::: {.cell}

$$\text{\color{purple}{Data}} = \text{\color{blue}{Model}} + \text{\color{red}{Error}}$$ {#eq-data-equals-model-plus-error}

I have no clear memory of where I first heard this phrase, but I have an idea that it was in the blog of [https://www.johndcook.com/](https://www.johndcook.com/).

The idea, as I have understood it, is that our [**observed data about the real world**]{fg="#800080"}, can be broken down into two parts: [**our model of the world**]{fg="#0000FF"}; and [**the ways in which our model is wrong**]{fg="#FF0000"}.

Consider a basic regression equation:

$$\color{purple}{y_i} \color{black}{=} \color{blue}{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i}} \color{black}{+} \color{red}{e_i}$$ {#eq-basic-regression-equation}

Broadly speaking, as we add independent variables (e.g. $x_2, x_3, \text{etc}...$) to the [**model**]{fg="#0000FF"} we reduce the amount of variation in $y_i$ that needs to be explained by the [**error**]{fg="#FF0000"}, $e_i$:  as the model gains more power, the error decreases.

This idea has specific implications for multilevel models, because multilevel models divide up the [**error**]{fg="#FF0000"} into pieces. For example $e_{ij}$ may become $e_{ij} + u_{0j}$. As the $x$'s in the model start to explain more and more of the variation in the dependent variable $y_{ij}$, the random intercept $u_{0j}$, possibly along with other random effects, often becomes less and less significant, and may ultimately become an *insignificant* part of the model. Put more intuitively: sometimes one starts with an unconditional multilevel model in which the random effects are a statistically significant part; as more and more $x$'s are added to the model, the random effects (e.g. $u_{0j}$) become less and less important and may even become statistically insignificant!
